new_fulltext_audits.title: DONIC: Generalist Dexterous Bimanual Tracking Control from Human Demonstrations
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. 3–6; main results/ablations; Appendices A–D, especially B.1, C.1–C.5 and D.1–D.6
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: Oct21 late-day boundary, not Oct22-window release. Success is joint tracking-threshold metric, not generic task completion. No real tactile policy or held-out operation/topology test.
new_fulltext_audits.artifact_status: Official arXiv full text inspected; external code/data release not independently verified.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: DONIC trains one reference-conditioned Wuji bimanual tracker using object-centered per-hand rewards and clip-centered advantages. Its BiHOI dataset adds 1,575 synchronized multi-view sequences; reported bilateral-contact proportions describe reconstructed contact-active frames, not measured tactile loading. The policy consumes object state, geometry and future hand/object references. Forty force-observation channels are zeroed; simulated net force plus proximity instead gates rewards, and cannot perfectly identify contact partners. On 53 unseen trajectories and 164 held-out-object clips, success is 86.79% and 57.32%, versus 9.43% and 11.59% for the stronger adapted baseline. Success combines generous hand/object trajectory-average thresholds, rather than independent semantic task completion. Baselines share the public pool and simulator but retain differing training/reward pipelines. Removing clip centering or the proximity contact-ownership condition reduces held-out-object success; adding BiHOI improves it to 59.76%. The contact ablation does not remove object-motion supervision. Reviewer inference: include as significant bimanual tracking/data evidence with useful controlled learning-signal ablations, not real tactile control or general goal-conditioned manipulation. Appendix D.6 explicitly excludes held-out operation-category claims. First submission is October21 at16:36:02UTC, so log it as a boundary/backlog discovery, not a new October22–28 release.

new_fulltext_audits.title: CW-WAM: A Structured Contact-Wrench World Action Model for Force-Sensitive Manipulation
new_fulltext_audits.authors: Ding, Houzhu and Qi, Xinda and Wang, Luqi and Yang, Ming
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. III-IV; V-A-G, Tables I-II and Figs. 4-7; VI limitations
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: Oct21 boundary release, not strict Oct22-onward first release. Bootstrap holds trained checkpoints fixed; hardware uses demonstration-distribution scenes. Force-reference accuracy is not independent contact-load truth.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: CW-WAM combines RGB, state, language and measured wrist-wrench history to predict paired motion/wrench chunks. Separate streams, pair-causal attention and ten-second wrench memory extend a shared world-action backbone; future targets are training supervision. Bias and calibrated tool-gravity compensation produce TCP-frame measurements, including payload load. Four tasks use 450 demonstrations. Matched-data, matched-schedule open-loop tests cover 373 windows from 22 test episodes: versus valid-normalized concatenation, the no-memory interaction module reduces contact-position error by 5.58 mm and dynamic force RMSE by 0.19 N, with paired episode-bootstrap confidence intervals. These intervals hold trained checkpoints fixed, not training seeds. Real tests remain within demonstration locations; peg/adapter insertion reaches 14/20 and 19/20, while the no-wrench baseline reaches 5/20 and 8/20. Added admittance improves successful-trial force-reference RMSE from 4.8 to 2.7 N for pegs without changing success. Model queries take 0.5–0.6 seconds; outer feedback is 20 Hz, not the 1-kHz joint tracker. This strengthens structured temporal-wrench and matched-loss baselines, but manually tuned task directions, shared-sensor force evaluation, selected successful subsets and no novel-object/task evaluation preclude cross-interface load identification or topology-transfer claims.

new_fulltext_audits.title: Live Thread Reconstruction for Autonomous Manipulation
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. II-A-F, III, IV; Table I; Figs.1-2
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: Graph orders thread geometry, not interhand load flow. Hard pickup 14/15 live versus 7/10 static; easy/medium 13/15 versus 18/20, with unmatched counts. Reconstruction error, occlusion robustness and detangling benchmarks remain future work; no force validation or topology holdout.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: Live Thread Reconstruction couples stereo keypoint adjacency/order with a spline-state extended Kalman filter, then selects constrained grasp points for two-arm manipulation. Tool motion predicts deformation; shape priors and confidence-weighted observations stabilize the spline. Hand-designed holder/receiver phases close the receiving grasp before release during knot tightening. Hard needle pickup improves from 7/10 static-reconstruction trials to 14/15 live trials, while easy/medium pickup is 18/20 versus 13/15; these unequal samples do not establish a universal gain. Knot tightening reports 15/15 easy/medium and 13/15 hard trials without a static comparator. Quantitative reconstruction, occlusion and detangling studies are explicitly ongoing, and epipolar-parallel segments remain problematic. This provides a geometric-state and role-gated regrasp baseline relevant to contact-rich coordination, but its adjacency graph represents thread shape rather than force transmission. No tactile sensing, tension ground truth, matched graph ablation, independent training seeds or held-out contact-participant structure is established.

new_fulltext_audits.title: PiHand: Latent Hand-Object Interaction Priors for Physics-Based Policy Learning
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. 3.1–3.3; 4.1–4.4; Appendices A–E, especially D.5 handover filtering and E.3–E.4
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: Handover51.9% is conditional on160 stable starts filtered from1442, not all candidate starts. New task policies train20h; prior reuse is not zero-shot policy transfer.
new_fulltext_audits.artifact_status: Official arXiv full text inspected; external code/data release not independently verified.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: PiHand distills physics-based hand-object tracking experts into a conditional latent prior, then trains task-specific residual policies within that space. Runtime generation discards future hand references but still uses simulator state, contact indicators, object geometry and future object trajectories. Binary body-contact signals are not measured tactile forces; intra-hand collisions are disabled partly because aggregate force readings cannot identify the contact partner. Held-out-object manipulation improves over action-space and hand-only-prior baselines, supporting interaction-aware priors within the common simulator and embodiment. For handover, reported success is 51.9% versus 11.9% and 5.0%. However, Appendix D.5 first screens 1,442 candidate starts with a policy-independent stability test, retains only 160, and evaluates one episode per retained start. The percentage is therefore conditional on stable initialization, not unconditional transfer reliability. Handover also receives a newly trained policy, explicit object-path and wrist-zone constraints, and twenty hours of task training; reusing a prior is not zero-shot policy deployment. Reviewer inference: include as dexterous handover and contact-aware latent evidence, while retaining denominator, reference-conditioning and simulator assumptions. Neither independent physical load measurement, real hardware validation nor a contact-topology-defined held-out test is demonstrated.

new_fulltext_audits.title: GelSlim 5.0: Unifying Vision and Touch with a Single Fingertip Camera
new_fulltext_audits.authors: Wang, Xiangdong and Huang, I-Hsuan and Xu, Xiaohao and Yi, Xili and Fazeli, Nima and Huang, Xiaonan
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. III, IV-A-E, V-A-C, VI; Tables II-III; Fig. 5-6 training ablations
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: Every tenth within-session sample is validation and checkpoint selection; computed geometric targets are not independently measured membrane shape. Fusion comparison differs in token/parameter budget; no cross-session/object/topology test.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: GelSlim 5.0 alternates UV illumination to obtain vision and tactile images from one fixed camera under approximately stationary contact. VisTacFusion combines frozen visual/tactile encoders through an asymmetric bottleneck, preserving spatial tactile features for depth/normals and supplying object identity to pose queries. Twelve objects provide approximately 400 contacts each; every tenth within-session sample serves both validation and checkpoint selection. Pose and known object geometry generate depth targets, rather than independent membrane-shape measurements. Paired input achieves 0.0066 mm2 depth MSE and 0.652-degree angular error, improving over either modality in the same selected model. Geometry and pose nevertheless use separate task-selected checkpoints. A matched-encoder/head symmetric-fusion comparison favors asymmetric fusion for pose but symmetric fusion for depth/normals; token counts and trainable parameters differ. Real/synthetic mixing also changes training duration and update count, so its gains do not isolate synthetic coverage. This is relevant contact-state/representation evidence, not closed-loop manipulation, unseen-object or cross-session generalization, physical force measurement, or topology transfer. Spatial correspondence avoids inter-camera extrinsics, but deformation, refraction and sequential motion remain. Main-table uncertainty is not established by the separate two-seed hyperparameter sweep.
new_fulltext_audits.artifact_status: Official full text accessible. Linked project https://gelslim5.github.io/ returned404 during audit; no code/data availability inferred.
new_fulltext_audits.relevance: Useful common-view geometry representation with clear observability, target-provenance and split limitations; eligible despite absence of closed-loop task.

new_fulltext_audits.title: VecTile: A Low-Cost Flexible Tactile Array for 3-DoF Force Sensing
new_fulltext_audits.authors: Hou, Jian and Zhou, Xin and Spiers, Adam J.
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. III-B, IV-B-D, V-A-B, VI; Tables II-III; four-fold direction-rotation split and multi-nub validation
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: Force RMSE uses held-out shear directions; plug holdout is unseen locations within training spatial range. Correction rates have conditional denominators. No bimanual/topology transfer or repeated-training-seed uncertainty.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: VecTile converts normal and tangential loading into four pressure-quadrant readings beneath each silicone nub. A quadratic per-taxel decoder is fitted against ATI Mini40 force labels. Four-fold held-out shear-direction tests produce 0.39 N normal and 0.16 N shear RMSE over 1-5 N normal and up to 1.5 N shear; reported variability is across 16 taxels, not independent sensor builds. Flat-calibrated decoding is tested on convex/concave mounts, and manual calibration is separately evaluated on new contacts and summed multi-nub loads. A 20-trial shear-triggered scalpel reflex prevents puncture, unlike a matched normal threshold. For plug insertion, 84 demonstrations train Diffusion Policy with two RGB streams, proprioception and 16 PCA components from touch. At unseen socket locations within the training range, full three-axis touch succeeds in 22/25 trials versus 16/25 normal-only and 12/25 vision-only. The 18/21 successful-correction result is conditional on failed direct insertion. This supports calibrated local shear and compact policy features, not bimanual load-path inference or topology transfer. No repeated-training-seed uncertainty is reported; force saturation, hysteresis/drift and durability remain limitations. The 343-Hz sensor stream is distinct from 10-Hz policy execution.
new_fulltext_audits.artifact_status: Official project explicitly says under review; code/hardware upon acceptance, not currently verified as released. arXiv comments identify ICRA2027 submission, not acceptance.
new_fulltext_audits.relevance: Independent force-label provenance and held-out direction calibration strengthen positive sensor-physics evidence; shear versus normal input comparison is relevant control baseline.

new_fulltext_audits.title: OpenTac: An Open Ecosystem for Customizable, Scalable, and Transferable 3D Tactile Sensing
new_fulltext_audits.authors: Slepyan, Ariel and Bethala, Geeta Chandra Raju and Gu, Jiafeng and Dangle, Anagha Rajendra and Zhou, Yinzhe and Fu, Hongyuan and Sim, Jade and Basu, Tuhin and Yin, Xinyi and Karim, Md Faizal and Hager, Gregory and Bharadhwaj, Homanga and Bhattad, Anand and Jatavallabhula, Krishna Murthy and Thakor, Nitish V.
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. 3.1-3.5, 4.1-4.8; Eq. 2; Table 2; PDF pp. 9-11 Figs. 11-12 visually checked; official project Results page
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: Force-fit accuracy is in-sample; transfer tests normal-contact shape, not force or policy transfer. Insertion rates conflict between paper figure/prose and live project; retain qualitative evidence and undisputed cup counts.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: OpenTac combines mechanically encoded normal/shear readings with a sensor manifest that anchors taxels, bump groups and local frames. Calibrated normal fields are transferred by geometric overlap with known contact pose. Across four skins, 5,290 predictions yield median shape F1 0.750 versus 0.714/0.634 resizing baselines; this evaluates contact shape, not force accuracy or policy transfer. Three-axis reference-force fits are explicitly in-sample. Real policies use proprioception and touch without vision, and bimanual key insertion senses only the key-holding gripper. More decisive load-related evidence comes from matched-trajectory cup holding: shear feedback retains the cup for 40 seconds in 16/20 impulsive-load trials, versus 9/20 with wrist F/T or normal-pressure feedback. These results support useful spatial shear sensing, not independently validated cross-interface load identification or topology-defined transfer. Insertion numbers require caution: v1 PDF/HTML reports 70% versus 54% for plug insertion, whereas the official project reports 62% versus 36%; key-in-lock prose says 62%, its figure 61%, despite a 25-trial caption. Bumps also change contact mechanics. Adaptive 1,286-Hz acquisition samples only 16/1,024 taxels per update, not the full field.
new_fulltext_audits.artifact_status: Official project and public code repository accessible; code not executed and data completeness not verified. CoRL live demo notice is not acceptance evidence.

new_fulltext_audits.relevance: Positive bimanual shear-feedback comparator; calibration/transfer scope and source-consistency audit materially refine review.

new_fulltext_audits.title: FORCA: A Force-Aware Coding Agent for Contact-Rich Robot Manipulation
new_fulltext_audits.authors: Tan, Xiao and Wang, Yixuan and Wang, Zhexi and Yuan, Wenzhen
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. III-A-C; IV-A-D, Tables I-V; V limitations
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: No demonstrations or task-specific model training, but up to20 real development rollouts and human-authorized execution. Removing force affects development, revision and execution together, not isolated online feedback.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: FORCA uses a foundation-model coding agent to write complete force-responsive programs from RGB-D, robot state and wrist wrench. Human-assembled perception, grasping and motion skills initialize the system. A generated 100-Hz feedback loop executes without foundation-model queries; the agent analyzes video and force traces and revises code between rollouts. Development permits twenty real rollouts or four hours, with human execution authorization and resets. Frozen programs are then evaluated: drawer and door operation each succeed in 10/10 trials, versus 4/10 and 1/10 for the same agent without force access. Static-developed wiping transfers to a human-moved vase with 93% mean mark removal and 1.6% contact-loss time, versus 21% and 55.9%, over ten trials. Peeling reaches 81.1% mean peeled length, not binary success. Contact-loss and excess-force fractions use explicitly thresholded active-task time. The no-force comparison removes sensing during synthesis, revision and execution together, so it measures the whole force-enabled workflow. Reasoning costs four to ten minutes per iteration; one door-development history is not repeated-run reliability. The study strengthens executable force-feedback and human-held-workpiece baselines, but wrist wrench cannot localize finger loads, and neither contact-graph inference nor held-out topology transfer is demonstrated.

new_fulltext_audits.title: CoCarry: Contact-Support-Structured Retargeting for Dual-Humanoid Cooperative Carrying
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. III–V; Tables I–II; contact metrics and CORE4D shared-success subset
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: 100% retargeting success is valid trajectory generation, not physical control success. Contact metric can remain high despite penetration; CORE4D compares shared-success subset with adapted mappings.
new_fulltext_audits.artifact_status: Paper states dataset/tools release is planned; no independently verified complete release claim.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: CoCarry releases a retargeting formulation with 220 two-person motion-capture sequences spanning 21 schemes, five objects and four terrains. It separates an object-relative upper-body relational mesh from ground-relative lower-body support structure, and adds hand-object anchors plus collision constraints around a prescribed object trajectory. Contacts are derived from geometry and motion, not measured touch, force or friction. Across all 220 source sequences, reported contact preservation is 0.9995 and penetration duration improves substantially over baselines. Yet the anchor ablation retains contact preservation of 0.9994 while penetration worsens sharply: proximity-based contact scoring alone is insufficient evidence of physical consistency. “100% success” denotes valid retargeted trajectories, not task execution. CORE4D comparisons use 200 shared-success sequences with adapted robot models and semantic mappings, rather than zero-shot control transfer. Real dual-humanoid carrying is qualitative; dataset-wide closed-loop success, trial counts and load measurements are not established. Reviewer inference: the study strengthens explicit contact/support decomposition and cooperative-motion dataset coverage, including changing hand participation. It does not validate independent cross-interface load labels or deployment-observable topology transfer. Prescribed object paths, contact thresholds and lower penetration being imperfectly aligned with contact scores should remain explicit.

new_fulltext_audits.title: Open-World Law-to-Action: Vision-Language Priors and Touch for Parts with Hidden Physics
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: All experiments simulated, including the physical robot; VLM latency cached/simulated. Final70/100 vs62/100 is not significant and follows controller/scoring changes between held-out tests.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: L 2 A converts vision-language declarations into floored priors over motion-law blocks, ranges and locks, then updates explicit Bayesian regressions from force and motion. Analytic results show that one-direction motion cannot separate constant load from Coulomb friction and that probing known motions cannot distinguish an unseen releaser from a jam; reversals and new views address different ambiguities. All experiments, including the mobile Panda, are MuJoCo simulations. Table 3 documents progressively removing privileged part identities, joints, coordinates and floor maps. Known-part and mixed-scene ablations support the within-agent mechanism: additional looks increase successes from 284/366 to 329/366. The final camera/depth/hand-based system completes 70/100 requests versus 62/100 for the partly simulator-assisted comparator, but this difference is not significant and follows a controller change and revised closing rule between two held-out tests. VLM answers are cached and latency simulated; part-motion declarations happen to be correct in that final test. Tasks share scenes, and some episode-level significance disappears at scene level. The work supports observability-aware physical inference and explicit assumption reporting, not hardware validation, arbitrary physics discovery, or superiority to matched learned policies. Its model-dependent safety guarantee excludes arbitrary model error; no robotic cross-interface load graph or strict contact-topology holdout is established.

new_fulltext_audits.title: How High Can GPT-6 Astra Climb in Contact-Rich Manipulation? PhysLadder: A Hierarchical, Matched Sim-Real Benchmark for Physical Interaction
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. 3-6; Tables 1-2; Appendices A-C, especially C.2-C.3; PDF pp.29-31
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: Three trials per task/environment; hierarchy depends on task version and embodiment. Simulation budgets and automatic assessment differ from unlimited real episodes and visual judgment. No tactile ablation, calibrated force validation, or topology-held-out transfer.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: PhysLadder organizes 16 tasks by alignment, sustained force regulation, and force regulation with required contact reconfiguration. Its two-arm gripper platform supplies RGB, proprioception and execution feedback, but no depth or dedicated force measurements. Fixed interface guidance differs between real and simulated execution. With three trials per task/environment, observed real success declines from 12/15 at L1 through 10/21 at L2 to 0/12 at L3; simulated counts are 10/15, 10/21 and 0/12. These are descriptive results for one model, not population reliability or an absolute task-difficulty law. Simulation has a 150-call/five-hour cap; hardware has no preset episode budget. Real visual judgments and simulated tolerances also differ, explicitly affecting alignment and wiping. The study strengthens task-version specifications and the distinction between local contact progress and full completion. It neither identifies forces independently nor isolates sensing, reasoning and execution causes; reconfiguration tasks alone do not constitute a held-out contact-topology generalization test.

new_fulltext_audits.title: 3D-Force Estimation for Dual-arm Manipulation of Deformable Linear Objects via Factor Graphs
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. II–IV; IV-A1–6; IV-B; Tables I–II; V–VI
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: Synthetic truth and observations derive from the same mechanics model; no hardware, matched comparator or calibrated posterior uncertainty. Explicit single-contact assumptions remain.
new_fulltext_audits.artifact_status: Trajectory data are stated to be available upon request; no public data/code artifact independently verified.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: This factor-graph estimator jointly reconstructs a deformable rod and one external force from sparse positional observations. Twenty rod-state nodes encode poses and internal wrenches; mechanics, boundary-pose and measurement factors couple them to unknown force magnitude, direction and location. Known homogeneous Kirchhoff material properties, quasi-static equilibrium, fixed end poses and a narrow Gaussian contact model provide substantial structure. Evaluation uses nine synthetic noisy marker positions derived from the same mechanics model, not a real camera or force sensor. Two ten-step pull/push trajectories report force-component mean errors of 0.008–0.022 N and location errors of 2.2–2.4 cm. These are model-consistency results, not independent physical grounding. No matched non-graph baseline, repeated-noise uncertainty study, posterior calibration, changing contact count, or closed-loop hardware control is demonstrated; experimental validation is explicitly future work. Torsion increases bias, and the authors suggest additional wrench sensing for torsion-dominant tasks. Reviewer inference: include as a directly relevant explicit mechanics/factor-graph formulation for dual-arm contact estimation, but do not upgrade assumed marker access to deployed observability or probabilistic notation to validated uncertainty. Shape-error units are inconsistent between pull and push prose, so avoid recycling those values without correction.

new_fulltext_audits.title: DEX-PHD: A Dexterous Portable Handheld Device for Multimodal Data Collection
new_fulltext_audits.authors: Hong, Jooyoung and Myers, Noboru and Kwon, Obin and Yang, Yixian and Kim, Joohyung
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. III-A-D; IV-A-E, Tables I-II; V limitations
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: Ten demos/task, lowest-IK-error feasible episode chosen and replayed once. Contact signals are baseline-relative, not independently calibrated force. Drill replay evaluates in-air actuation, not full fastening.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: DEX-PHD integrates a six-actuated-DOF robotic hand with per-finger triggers, thirty FSR channels and wrist video. Hand commands, measured states and contact signals are logged at 100 Hz, video at 60 fps; LED events align streams to tens-of-milliseconds resolution, with rolling QR alignment for two-device recording. Wrist SLAM and embodiment-specific inverse kinematics/offsets transfer trajectories while retaining the same hands. This is portable robot-hand data collection, not learned tactile control. For each of three tasks, ten demonstrations were collected, the feasible episode with lowest inverse-kinematics tracking error selected, and that episode replayed once on a humanoid. The reported metrics therefore do not estimate success rates or repeated-execution variability. Insertion has 2.66-degree joint MAE but only 0.197 contact correlation, directly showing that kinematic replay agreement does not guarantee contact reproduction. Multi-object grasping and drill actuation have contact correlations 0.691 and 0.761. FSR values are baseline-subtracted and aggregated per finger, not independent absolute-force measurements. Physical drill analysis covers in-air grasp/trigger motion because full fastening was difficult to reproduce reliably. The study supplies a useful contact-aware replay diagnostic and portable recording interface, but does not establish closed-loop tactile benefit, cross-hand hardware transfer, reproducible task reliability or load-path/topology generalization.

new_fulltext_audits.title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. III-A-C, IV-A-F; Tables I-II; real-world force-tracking paragraph
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: External gauge validates standalone force tracking, not all simultaneous task load paths. Same-network force-command withholding is an execution intervention; observation removal is retrained. Ten paired-condition rollouts per task, no topology-held-out or matched graph-versus-latent test.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: FLoRe combines robot-free bilateral wrist-wrench demonstrations, a causal force-history diffusion policy, and hybrid whole-body force/position control. Per-hand force commands and measured feedback drive a shared controller; an external digital gauge validates standalone hardware tracking, with about 1.1 N reported steady-state error along the x axis. On gantry pushing, bimanual box rotation and wiping, ten condition-matched trials/task yield 24/30 successes versus 8/30 for a position-only policy trained with the same architecture/data/schedule. Withholding commands from the same trained force policy yields 11/30; retraining without force observations yields 20/30. Thus execution of predicted force has stronger evidence than an isolated representation advantage. Simulator force statistics condition on paired non-falling clips; physical tests remain one platform and limited masses, poses and surfaces. This is positive evidence for independently checked force control and bimanual load coordination, not a learned inter-interface graph or identification of every simultaneous load path. No contact-topology holdout or matched structural-representation comparison is reported.

new_fulltext_audits.title: CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. 3.1-3.5, 4.1-4.5; Tables 1-3; Appendices A-I; PDF pp.7,13,20
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: Offline future-containing targets; glove pressure distinct from inconsistently documented mocap pressure/proximity and mesh use. Physics task/run rates have unspecified valid-run denominators; no pooled effect. Identical-trajectory force-controller ablation does not isolate learned contact-graph superiority.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: CARD transfers contact locations, directions and force targets through semantic human-to-robot link mappings. Video/GRAB forces are synthesized over entire clips; centered smoothing, synchronized onsets and pseudo-object construction use offline information. Measured glove pressure is a distinct source. Appendix A describes mocap pressure while Appendix H labels mocap proximity-based contact; Appendix D uses tracked meshes despite Appendix A saying evaluation-only. Source provenance and blanket object-free claims therefore need qualification. Geometric fidelity pools anchor-frames, not physical successes. Replaying identical trajectories with fingertip-force control yields 25/30 successes versus 4/30 position-only across three tasks. Four-embodiment retargeting uses explicit semantic maps; tactile-free hands need compliance or action scaling. The physics variant bundles changed initialization, objective and targets. Table 3 task rates and Appendix I run rates cannot be reconciled or pooled without the unspecified valid-run denominators after invalid-physics exclusion. This supports contact-preserving retargeting and local force feedback, not causal cross-interface load identification, matched learned-representation benefit, or topology OOD.

new_fulltext_audits.title: RoboSTD: Zero-Shot Single-to-Dual Transfer via Sagittal Mirroring for Bimanual Learning
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. IV-A–C; V-A–D; VI; Figs. 4–6; Appendix A mirror-mapping derivation
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: Zero-shot refers to not collecting task-specific bimanual demonstrations, not inference without training. LLM ablation bundles scheduling constraints and stage language; graph is semantic, not contact mechanics.
new_fulltext_audits.artifact_status: Official arXiv full text inspected; external code/data release not independently verified.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: RoboSTD constructs pseudo-bimanual demonstrations from single-arm data using sagittal mirroring of images, robot states and actions. The joint mapping depends on calibrated URDF axes and symmetric mounting, not universal sign flips. GPT-4.1 supplies arm assignments, precedence/conflict constraints and stage-language annotations; these describe semantic coordination rather than physical contact edges. Policies are fine-tuned on the constructed data, so “zero-shot” concerns the absence of additional task-specific bimanual demonstrations, not untrained inference. On ten RoboTwin tasks, success is 66.5% versus 39.1% for single-arm data and 67.6% for a native-bimanual oracle. Five real ALOHA tasks include coordinated stacking and sandwich making; sandwich completion reaches 74%, but whole-task success is 50%, illustrating the importance of preserving metric definitions. Removing the LLM reduces performance, but simultaneously removes coordination constraints and stage-language annotation, preventing attribution to graph structure alone. No tactile or force observations, physical load labels, or contact-topology-defined holdout are present. Trial/seed uncertainty is not clearly reported. Reviewer inference: include as evidence that data-level role and temporal structure can support real bimanual policies; do not equate semantic scheduling, symmetry-dependent augmentation, or target fine-tuning with physical contact representation or zero-shot embodiment transfer.

new_fulltext_audits.title: ActiveAlign: Aligning Egocentric Manipulation via Active Perception
new_fulltext_audits.authors: Qiu, Ri-Zhao and Wen, Bowen and Jiang, Yifeng and Tessler, Chen and Heiden, Eric and Peng, Xue Bin and Wang, Xiaolong and Birchfield, Stan and Coumans, Erwin
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: Tactile map plus custom motion primitives compared with keypoint planning; not a representation-only ablation.60Hz control thread and2FPS pose tracking differ; no calibrated force or topology-transfer test.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: ActiveAlign combines active hand-eye calibration with tactile refinement of object alignment. Offline robot/scene reconstruction supplies differentiable Gaussian-splat models and simulation assets; online RGB-D segmentation and pose tracking align them. Multi-state hand waving stabilizes camera estimation, while slowly probing a local planar panel until fingertip force crosses a threshold constructs an action-indexed height map. Real G 1 experiments use an eighty-element RoboSkin index-finger array and tactile-map-conditioned motion primitives. Across three panels, success is 14/20,9/20 and 15/20, compared with 3/20,2/20 and 8/20 for keypoint planning. This supports the integrated active-touch alignment pipeline, not an isolated learned-representation effect, because the planner/primitives also differ. Calibration experiments on public robot datasets improve mask overlap and cross-trajectory consistency; those tests do not establish tactile transfer across sensors or embodiments. AppendixB reports three-run calibration averages, but no comparable repeated-training uncertainty for manipulation. The control thread runs at 60 Hz while FoundationPose runs at 2 FPS, and the method requires offline assets and a local planar sampling assumption. ArUco fixtures provide evaluation references rather than runtime alignment. The work supplies a useful action-grounded geometric-contact baseline and highlights accumulated perception/kinematic error, without identifying calibrated loads, interhand contact structure, or held-out contact-topology generalization.

new_fulltext_audits.title: Keeping Contact: Task-Adaptive Friction Margins for Bimanual Non-Prehensile Manipulation
new_fulltext_audits.evidence_locator: Secs. III-A–E; Eqs. 3–28; IV-A/B; V-A–E; Tables I–II
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: Task-adaptive margins pass 5/5 per condition; measured margin violations remain nonzero. Fixed-margin comparator matched average planned force; no contact-mode transfer or independent pivot-load labels.
new_fulltext_audits.artifact_status: Project link https://keeping-contact.github.io/ was not accessible during this pass; publisher acceptance record not located.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: Two Kinova arms tilt a shared box about an environmental pivot using contact-specific friction margins and a convex quasi-static force planner. Known geometry, friction, mass and contact modes supply the structural prior; ATI wrist sensors measure actual forces, rather than learned tactile features. The adaptive allocation accounts for moment sensitivity and changing support/braking roles. Each of eight conditions has five trials, all successful with adaptive margins. Crucially, the fixed-margin comparator is calibrated per condition to match average combined planned force, so improved robustness cannot be reduced simply to exerting more force. Under a negative center-of-mass mismatch, adaptive margins succeed in 5/5 versus 0/5 for fixed margins. Nevertheless, completion does not imply zero constraint violation: nominal measured violation is 6.9%, and model/controller discrepancies remain. Small samples and no confidence analysis limit reliability claims. Reviewer inference: this is a genuine real bilateral-force redistribution baseline and counterevidence against blanket claims that such physical control evidence is absent. It is not an inferred cross-interface tactile graph, independently measured pivot reaction, online mode discovery, or held-out topology-transfer experiment. ArXiv comments claim RA-L acceptance; without publisher corroboration, retain explicitly author-claimed status.

new_fulltext_audits.title: Which Hand Was Late? Diagnosis for Robot Failure Recovery in Bimanual Tool Use
new_fulltext_audits.coding_note: Canonical timing result reverses under randomized onsets; hidden force threshold remains unidentifiable. No real robot or topology-defined transfer.
new_fulltext_audits.artifact_status: Official arXiv full text inspected; external code/data release not independently verified.
new_fulltext_audits.audit_summary: Two simulated Panda arms jointly turn a spring-return lock with a key-tool and push a door. Mechanism traces label failures, while grouped-by-door probes compare wrist wrench, proprioception, commands and images. The hidden latch-force threshold is unavailable to sensing; contact and mechanism oracles must not be conflated with robot-like channels. Under the canonical schedule, bilateral joint positions diagnose coordination failures with pooled AUC 0.986, while tool wrist torque diagnoses cam-out at 0.972. However, Appendix B independently randomizes onset times: bilateral-pose probes fall to approximately chance, whereas explicit relative-onset features remain strong. This materially limits any generic bilateral-representation claim. In 386 blocked replay attempts, diagnosis-aware escalation repairs 297 within two attempts versus 211 for a single-label strategy, while making fewer hard pushes than an all-at-once repair. These are simulator interventions, not demonstrated physical safety or real-world recovery. Door-group bootstrap intervals support the canonical diagnostic comparison, but do not remove schedule dependence or hidden-threshold ambiguity. Reviewer inference: include as tool-use identifiability and uncertainty evidence, emphasizing that uncertain cause sets and explicit temporal relations can matter more than a single confident failure label. It does not establish learned tactile topology transfer.
